title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: RDBMS Basics
summary: An RDBMS (Relational Database Management System) is the software that stores tables on disk, parses SQL, optimizes queries into execution plans, and executes them — internally structured as a parser, optimizer, executor, and…
objectives: Walk me through what happens inside an RDBMS when you run `SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = 42`.
What is the buffer pool, and why does its hit ratio matter so much?
What is MVCC, and what problem does it solve?
What is the difference between a logical plan and a physical plan?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** An RDBMS (Relational Database Management System) is the software that stores tables on disk, parses SQL, optimizes queries into execution plans, and executes them — internally structured as a parser, optimizer, executor, and storage engine that communicate through a buffer pool and a transaction log.

When you send `SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = 42` to PostgreSQL, a surprising amount of machinery runs before you see a row. The query enters through the **parser**, which checks syntax and produces an abstract syntax tree (AST). The parser does not know or care whether `users` exists or whether `id` is a column — that is the **binder's** (or *analyzer's*) job, which resolves names against the system catalog (the metadata tables describing tables, columns, types, indexes, constraints) and produces a logical plan. The logical plan says "scan `users`, filter `id = 42`, project `name`" but does not say *how*. That is the **optimizer's** job: it enumerates physical alternatives — sequential scan, index scan, index-only scan, bitmap scan — estimates their cost using table statistics (row count, distribution of values, index depth), and picks the cheapest. The chosen plan is then handed to the **executor**, which runs it against the **storage engine**, fetching pages from the **buffer pool** (an in-memory cache of disk blocks) and returning result rows to the client.

The **storage engine** is the bottom of the stack and the most performance-sensitive component. Data on disk is organized into **pages** (also called blocks) of fixed size — typically 8 KB in PostgreSQL, 16 KB in MySQL/InnoDB. A page is the unit of I/O: even if you want one row, the database reads the entire page containing it into the buffer pool. Pages are organized into **extents** (groups of pages) and **segments** (tablespaces). Each page has a header (page LSN, checksum, free-space pointer), a row slot array, and the rows themselves packed from the end of the page backwards. When a row is updated, the storage engine does not overwrite — it writes a new version elsewhere and marks the old version as dead, leaving cleanup to a background **vacuum** process (PostgreSQL) or in-place updates with undo logs (InnoDB). This is the foundation of MVCC.

**MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)** is the technique that lets readers not block writers and writers not block readers. Each transaction sees a **snapshot** of the database as of the moment the transaction began (in `REPEATABLE READ`) or the moment the statement began (in `READ COMMITTED`). When a row is updated, the database creates a new version with a new `xmin` (transaction id that created it) and stamps the old version with an `xmax` (transaction id that deleted it); a reader determines whether a version is visible to its snapshot by comparing `xmin`/`xmax` against the set of transactions committed at snapshot time. The result is that a long-running `SELECT` sees a consistent view of the data even as other transactions write new versions concurrently — no locks held on the read path. The cost is dead tuples: old versions accumulate until vacuum reclaims them, which is why PostgreSQL has autovacuum and why long-running transactions (which prevent vacuum from reclaiming anything they might still see) cause table and index bloat.

Real-world: Netflix's billing system runs on PostgreSQL (Aurora PostgreSQL in AWS). Every month, ~230 million subscribers are billed, and each billing transaction touches `accounts`, `subscriptions`, `invoices`, `payment_attempts`, and `ledger_entries` tables. The workload is mixed: bursts of OLTP during the monthly billing run (millions of small UPDATE and INSERT statements per hour) and continuous read traffic from the customer-facing "My Account" page. MVCC is what makes this work — a customer viewing their invoice page (a long-running `SELECT` joining four tables) does not block the billing batch from updating `invoices.paid_at`, and the billing batch does not block the customer's view. The trade-off is operational: Netflix tunes autovacuum aggressively on the billing cluster (lower `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` on `invoices` so vacuum triggers earlier), runs `pg_repack` weekly on the largest tables to reclaim bloat without an exclusive lock, and monitors `pg_stat_activity` for long-running transactions that block vacuum. A billing transaction that hangs for an hour — perhaps stuck waiting on a downstream payment gateway — would prevent vacuum from reclaiming dead tuples, causing the table to grow until disk fills.

The **query execution plan** is the optimizer's output and the first place to look when a query is slow. `EXPLAIN` shows the plan; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and shows actual row counts and timing per node. A plan is a tree of operators: `Seq Scan`, `Index Scan`, `Index Only Scan`, `Bitmap Heap Scan`, `Hash Join`, `Nested Loop`, `Sort`, `Aggregate`. Each node has an estimated cost (`cost=0.42..8.45`) split into startup cost (work before producing the first row) and total cost, plus estimated row count and row width. Misestimates — when the optimizer thinks a table has 100 rows but it actually has 100 million — cause catastrophic plan choices, typically picking a Nested Loop join that explodes into billions of iterations. The fix is `ANALYZE` (updates statistics) or, in stubborn cases, hints (PostgreSQL's `pg_hint_plan`, or the manual `SET enable_nestloop = off` escape hatch). Understanding the plan tree is the single most valuable debugging skill for SQL performance.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[SQL query string] --> P[Parser: syntax check -> AST]
    P --> B[Binder/Analyzer: resolve names against catalog]
    B --> O[Optimizer: enumerate plans, pick cheapest]
    O --> E[Executor: runs plan, produces rows]
    E --> BP[Buffer Pool: 8KB page cache in RAM]
    BP -->|hit| R[(return rows)]
    BP -->|miss| D[(Disk: data files, indexes)]
    D --> BP
    E --> WAL[(WAL log: write-ahead for durability)]
    E --> R2[Client result set]

    B -.->|reads| C[(System Catalog: tables, columns, stats)]
    O -.->|reads| C
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
RDBMS internals: query lifecycle

  SQL: SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = 42;
   |
   v
+-------------------+   Parser    - syntax -> AST
| 1. Parser         |   Binder    - resolve names vs catalog
+-------------------+   Optimizer - cost-based plan selection
   |
   v  logical plan -> physical plan
+-------------------+
| 2. Optimizer      |   picks: Index Scan (cost=0.42..8.45)
+-------------------+           vs Seq Scan (cost=0.00..154.21)
   |
   v
+-------------------+
| 3. Executor       |   walks plan tree, fetches pages
+-------------------+
   |
   v
+-------------------+
| 4. Storage Engine |   buffer pool (RAM) <-> disk (8KB pages)
+-------------------+
   |
   v
  result rows back to client

Page layout (8KB block):
+-------------------------------------------+
| header (LSN, checksum, free space ptr)    |
|-------------------------------------------|
| row slot array: [ptr to row3, row2, row1] |
|-------------------------------------------|
| ... free space ...                         |
|-------------------------------------------|
| row1 | row2 | row3   (packed from end)    |
+-------------------------------------------+

MVCC: each row version has xmin (created by) and xmax (deleted by)
   txn 100 INSERTs row   -> xmin=100, xmax=NULL  (visible if 100 committed)
   txn 200 UPDATEs row   -> new version xmin=200, xmax=NULL
                          old version xmax=200    (dead once no snapshot sees it)
   vacuum later          -> physically removes xmax-set, no live snapshot
```

### Walkthrough
1. The parser converts SQL text into an AST; the binder resolves table and column names against the system catalog, producing a logical plan that says *what* to compute but not *how*.
2. The optimizer enumerates physical plans (sequential scan, index scan, join orders), estimates each plan's cost using table statistics, and picks the cheapest. Misestimates here cause slow queries.
3. The executor runs the plan: it asks the storage engine for pages, which are fetched from the buffer pool on hit or from disk on miss. MVCC ensures each transaction sees a consistent snapshot without locking writers, at the cost of accumulating dead tuples that vacuum must reclaim.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
RDBMS internals demo with sqlite3.

Shows: EXPLAIN (query plan output), page-level concepts via rowid,
statistics (ANALYZE), and an MVCC-like snapshot using BEGIN.

Run:  python3 rdbms_basics_demo.py
"""

import sqlite3, time

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")           # write-ahead logging
cur = conn.cursor()

# --- schema + data ---
cur.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE users (
    id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,        -- rowid alias; the physical page locator
    name  TEXT NOT NULL,
    city  TEXT NOT NULL,
    age   INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_city ON users(city);
""")
cur.executemany(
    "INSERT INTO users(id, name, city, age) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
    [(i, f"user_{i}", "NYC" if i % 3 == 0 else "SFO", 20 + (i % 50)) for i in range(1, 10001)],
)

# --- EXPLAIN: see the physical plan the optimizer chose ---
print("-- EXPLAIN: SELECT by indexed column (city) --")
for row in cur.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE city = 'NYC'"):
    print(" ", row)

print("\n-- EXPLAIN: SELECT by primary key (uses the rowid B-tree) --")
for row in cur.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = 42"):
    print(" ", row)

print("\n-- EXPLAIN: SELECT with no usable index (full table scan) --")
for row in cur.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 60"):
    print(" ", row)

# --- ANALYZE: refresh statistics the optimizer uses for cost estimates ---
cur.execute("ANALYZE users")
print("\n-- after ANALYZE: stats stored in sqlite_stat1 --")
for row in cur.execute("SELECT * FROM sqlite_stat1"):
    print(" ", row)

# --- Snapshot isolation demo (sqlite's analogue of MVCC) ---
print("\n-- snapshot isolation: reader sees pre-update state --")
reader = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)
reader.executescript("""
ATTACH DATABASE 'file::memory:?cache=shared' AS shared;
""")
# Easier: use a file-backed DB so two connections share data.
import os, tempfile
path = tempfile.mktemp(suffix=".db")
for c in (conn, reader):
    c.close()
shared = sqlite3.connect(path)
shared.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")
scur = shared.cursor()
scur.executescript("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS counter(n INTEGER); INSERT INTO counter VALUES(0);")
scur.execute("COMMIT")

r1 = sqlite3.connect(path)            # reader connection
w1 = sqlite3.connect(path)            # writer connection
r1.execute("BEGIN")                   # start a read snapshot
print("  reader sees n =", r1.execute("SELECT n FROM counter").fetchone()[0])

w1.execute("UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1")      # writer commits
print("  writer committed; n is now", w1.execute("SELECT n FROM counter").fetchone()[0])
print("  reader still sees n =", r1.execute("SELECT n FROM counter").fetchone()[0], "(snapshot)")
r1.execute("COMMIT")                              # end snapshot
print("  reader after COMMIT sees n =", r1.execute("SELECT n FROM counter").fetchone()[0])

os.unlink(path)
```

logical plan** describes what to compute — scan users, filter id = 42, project name, join with orders — without specifying how.

quiz.explanation: The buffer pool is an in-memory cache of disk pages (8 KB blocks in PostgreSQL, 16 KB in InnoDB) shared across all connections to the database. When the executor needs a page, it checks the buffer pool first; on a hit, it reads from RAM (microseconds), and on a miss, it issues a synchronous read from disk (milliseconds — 100–1000× slower).
